text: Every subscription has a Cost Management + Billing blade in the portal, where you go to answer what you're actually spending and on what. Two pieces matter most day to day: Cost analysis, which shows spend broken down different ways, and Budgets, which watch that spend against a threshold you set. Cost analysis is the view; Budgets is the watchdog.

Cost analysis lets you filter or group spend by resource group, service, location, or — this is where Chapter 1's tagging discipline pays off directly — tag. Tag every resource in a project the same way when it's created, and Cost analysis can show exactly what that project costs across every resource group it touches, something a resource-group-only view can't do cleanly once a project spans more than one group.

A budget is a spend threshold set for a scope, a subscription or a resource group, over a period, almost always monthly. Here's the detail that trips people up: a budget does not stop spending on its own. It's an alerting mechanism. You set alert thresholds — a percentage of the budget — and crossing one sends a notification. Keeping a resource running past 100% of its budget is entirely possible; the budget just makes sure someone finds out.

Say a resource group's VMs, storage, and networking are expected to cost about $500 a month. Set a budget scoped to that group: amount $500, period monthly, alert thresholds at 80% and 100%. Hit $400 mid-month and an email goes out — real warning to investigate before the month closes, instead of finding out when the invoice already says $700.

Metrics, logs, the Activity Log, alerts and Action Groups, and now budgets — this chapter covered every real way Azure tells you what's happening right now and what it's costing you along the way. Chapter 8 puts all of it to work in a hands-on capstone, starting with a lab deploying a small multi-tier environment from the ground up.
